findings.summary: The section does not cover an outline point (missing "authentication", "authorization").
findings.evidence: Definition: IAM is the global AWS service that decides who (authentication) can do what on which resource (authorization); principals are users, roles and the root account
findings.fix: Add the point with an explanation and an example.

findings.summary: Access Analyzer and last accessed data are named as the answer to 'what permissions does a role really use' but never explained.
findings.evidence: 'Real permissions used? Access Analyzer, last accessed data'
findings.fix: Add one line saying last accessed data shows which services and actions an identity actually called, and Access Analyzer can generate a least-privilege policy from CloudTrail activity. Use that to trim unused permissions.

findings.summary: One bullet holds two ideas: the Deny conditions and the override rule.
findings.evidence: "Deny on aws:SourceIp or MFA false blocks access even if another policy allows it"
findings.fix: Split it into two bullets: "Deny can use conditions such as aws:SourceIp or MFA false" and "A matching Deny blocks access even if another policy allows it".

findings.summary: The section does not cover an outline point (missing "definition", "security").
findings.evidence: Definition: MFA adds a second factor (virtual TOTP app, FIDO2 security key or hardware token) on top of the password; the root account is the all-powerful email-based identity created with the account
findings.fix: Add the point with an explanation and an example.

findings.summary: The section does not cover an outline point (missing "automatically", "credentials").
findings.evidence: Comparison: access keys are long-lived (AKIA...) and leak through code and git; role credentials are temporary (ASIA... plus session token) and expire automatically, so prefer roles for EC2, Lambda and CI
findings.fix: Add the point with an explanation and an example.

findings.summary: The section does not cover an outline point (missing "applications", "credentials").
findings.evidence: Interview Point: Why should the root account have no access keys? When do you still need an access key? How do you enforce MFA with a policy? How do applications on EC2 get credentials without keys?
findings.fix: Add the point with an explanation and an example.

findings.summary: The outline's interview points for this section are missing: why root gets no keys, when an access key is still needed, and how EC2 apps get credentials without keys.
findings.evidence: Page 3 has sections 1-4 plus a 'Keys hygiene' note and no interview block. The only hint is the table row 'Use for | local CLI only'.
findings.fix: Add an 'Interview Point' block. Cover: root keys give full-account power and cannot be scoped; keys are still needed for local CLI or external systems that cannot assume a role; EC2 apps get credentials from an instance profile role via STS.

findings.summary: The key-rotation rule sits under the "Example: Enforce MFA" section after the code, so it is unrelated to that section and easy to miss.
findings.evidence: "4. Example: Enforce MFA ... Keys hygiene Rotate or delete any access key unused for 90 days."
findings.fix: Move the rule into section 3 "Keys vs Roles" or into its own numbered section.

findings.summary: The Root-only bullet packs several separate tasks into one line.
findings.evidence: "Root-only: change root email or password, close account, restore locked-out IAM admin"
findings.fix: Make it a short list with one task per bullet.

findings.summary: The heading "Policy Types" is reused for a different classification than page 2 (managed vs inline instead of identity vs resource-based), which can confuse a learner skimming for the term.
findings.evidence: Page 2: "2. Policy types ... Identity-based | Resource-based | Permission boundary | SCP" vs page 4: "2. Policy Types ... AWS managed | Customer managed | Inline"
findings.fix: Rename page 4's section to "Managed vs Inline Policies" and page 2's to "Policy Types by Scope".

findings.summary: The cheat sheet says everyone else should use roles or IAM Identity Center, but page 3 says daily work uses an IAM user or IAM Identity Center.
findings.evidence: Page 3: "Daily work: IAM user or IAM Identity Center" vs page 5: "Everyone else: roles or IAM Identity Center"
findings.fix: Use the same wording on both pages, for example "Daily work: IAM Identity Center or roles; IAM users only when needed".

findings.summary: The quiz answer depends on the service principal ec2.amazonaws.com, which the chapter never teaches. Trust policy is also used on pages 1 and 4 before it is defined.
findings.evidence: 'The trust policy must name ec2.amazonaws.com as Principal.' Page 1 only says 'Principals named in its trust policy', and page 4 says 'Role needs a trust policy and a permissions policy'.
findings.fix: On page 1 or 4, define a trust policy as the resource-based policy on a role that names who may assume it. Show a short example with Principal {"Service":"ec2.amazonaws.com"} and Action sts:AssumeRole.

findings.summary: The section does not cover an outline point (missing "geographic", "resources").
findings.evidence: A Region is an isolated geographic area with 3+ AZs; an AZ is one or more data centres. Most resources are regional or AZ-scoped, and IAM is global.
findings.fix: Add the point with an explanation and an example.

findings.summary: The section does not cover an outline point (missing "private", "network").
findings.evidence: A VPC is your private network inside one Region and spans all its AZs. Pick a primary CIDR between /16 and /28, such as 10.0.0.0/16, and keep it clear of other VPCs and on-prem ranges.
findings.fix: Add the point with an explanation and an example.

findings.summary: CIDR is used in the scope map and mistakes before any explanation of what it is or what /16 or /28 means.
findings.evidence: "Primary CIDR between /16 and /28, e.g. 10.0.0.0/16" and "Why CIDR for peering? Overlapping ranges cannot be routed."
findings.fix: Add a short line to the scope map: CIDR is an IP range written as address/prefix length; a smaller number means a bigger range, so /16 is about 65k addresses and /28 is 16.

findings.summary: The CIDR bullets are tacked onto the scope table, and the mistakes are fragments with no stated consequence.
findings.evidence: "Primary CIDR between /16 and /28, e.g. 10.0.0.0/16" after the table; "Default VPC used for production"
findings.fix: Give CIDR its own short heading, and phrase each mistake with its consequence, e.g. 'Default VPC in production: no deliberate CIDR or subnet design'.

findings.summary: The section does not cover an outline point (missing "automatically", "horizontally").
findings.evidence: An IGW is free, horizontally scaled, and lets instances reach the internet only if they also have a public or Elastic IP. A zonal NAT gateway sits in a public subnet with an Elastic IP (a regional NAT gateway needs no public subnet and spans AZs automatically) and gives private subnets outbound-only internet via 0.0.0.0/0 -> nat-id.
findings.fix: Add the point with an explanation and an example.

findings.summary: One bullet packs two unrelated rules, and the public/private definition is split across bullets.
findings.evidence: "One route table per subnet; longest prefix wins"
findings.fix: Split into two bullets: one route table per subnet, and longest prefix wins.

findings.summary: "Ephemeral ports" is used as the reason NACLs need a return-traffic rule, but the chapter never says what they are.
findings.evidence: "Stateless: allow replies, ports 1024-65535" and "A custom NACL without the outbound ephemeral range breaks replies." Page 6 then relies on it: "replies leave on the client's ephemeral port."
findings.fix: On page 3, add one line: the client picks a random high port (1024-65535) as its source port, and the server's reply goes back to that port, so a stateless NACL must allow that range outbound.

findings.summary: Bullets hold more than one idea, and the SG/NACL example diagram has no visible flow or direction.
findings.evidence: "Allow only; default deny in, allow all out"; "Stateless: allow replies, ports 1024-65535"; "Internet / Web SG / DB SG"
findings.fix: Split each into one-idea bullets, and draw the example as Internet -> Web SG (443) -> DB SG (5432 from web-SG) with arrows.

findings.summary: The T-type credit behaviour is stated twice with slightly different instance lists, and a third time in the interview point.
findings.evidence: "T-types burst on CPU credits; standard mode throttles when empty, unlimited (T3/T4g default) bills surplus" / "Unlimited mode (T3/T3a/T4g/T8i) bills surplus" / "Credits out? Standard: throttles to baseline. Unlimited (T3/T3a/T4g default)..."
findings.fix: State it once as a two-row Standard vs Unlimited table with a single instance list, and keep one short interview line.

findings.summary: The page is overloaded and mixes topics. A launch-checklist bullet sits inside the pricing block, and the mistakes are one prose sentence holding three ideas.
findings.evidence: "Launch with SG, key pair, subnet, IAM instance profile, not keys" under Pricing; "Stopped instances still pay for EBS; unattached Elastic IPs bill; Spot is wrong for stateful databases."
findings.fix: Move the launch bullet under AMIs or a short Launch heading, and split the mistakes into three one-line bullets.

findings.summary: The troubleshooting chain is written as one dense line where a layered diagram or list would be easier to scan.
findings.evidence: "Internet to private DB: IGW (not attached), route table (no route), NACL (deny, no ephemeral ports), SG (no allow rule), instance (not listening)."
findings.fix: Show it as an ordered list or a flow: IGW -> route table -> NACL -> SG -> instance, with the failure cause on each line.

findings.summary: The explanation of why the outbound-443-only NACL breaks replies is worded backwards: replies leave from port 443 and are addressed to the client's ephemeral port.
findings.evidence: NACLs are stateless: replies leave on the client's ephemeral port.
findings.fix: Reword to: "NACLs are stateless: replies go from port 443 to the client's ephemeral port, so the outbound rule must allow destination ports 1024-65535."

findings.summary: The Everyday Commands section shows four commands with no line first saying what they do.
findings.evidence:
3. Everyday Commands
bash
aws s3 cp file s3://bucket/key
aws s3 ls s3://bucket/prefix/
findings.fix: Add a one-line idea before the code block, e.g. 'cp uploads, ls lists, sync mirrors a folder, rm deletes by prefix'. Or put a short comment above each command.

findings.summary: The blanket claim that archived objects need a restore before GET is wrong for Glacier Instant Retrieval, which serves reads in milliseconds.
findings.evidence: "Archived objects need a restore before GET" appears directly under a table where Glacier Instant is listed with "Get: ms". Page 1 and page 6 repeat the same line next to "Glacier Instant / Flexible".
findings.fix: Say "Glacier Flexible Retrieval and Deep Archive objects need a restore before GET; Glacier Instant Retrieval is read directly in milliseconds." Make the same change on pages 1 and 6.

findings.summary: The Deep Archive retrieval times '~12h / ~48h' are never labeled as Standard and Bulk, so a learner cannot tell which tier each number belongs to.
findings.evidence: Deep Archive | archive | 180d | ~12h / ~48h
findings.fix: Write 'Standard ~12h / Bulk ~48h' in the Get column, and give the Flexible tiers rough times (Expedited minutes, Standard hours, Bulk longer) so the Expedited/Standard/Bulk list has meaning.

findings.summary: NoncurrentVersionExpiration and 'old versions' are used before versioning, current versus noncurrent, and delete markers are introduced on page 4.
findings.evidence: Also set AbortIncompleteMultipartUpload, NoncurrentVersionExpiration ... Old versions? Expire noncurrent versions
findings.fix: Add a one-line gloss on page 3, e.g. 'noncurrent = an older version kept after an overwrite or delete (see Versioning)', or move that rule to page 4.

findings.summary: The Get column and the retrieval tiers are shown without saying what they mean, so the '~12h / ~48h' values can't be read.
findings.evidence: Deep Archive | archive | 180d | ~12h / ~48h ... Flexible: Expedited, Standard, Bulk
findings.fix: Rename the column to 'Retrieval time'. Label the Deep Archive values (Standard ~12h, Bulk ~48h). Give a speed for each Flexible tier or drop the tier list.

findings.summary: The code block comes before its one-line explanation, and the explanation line is orphaned after it.
findings.evidence:
aws s3api list-object-versions --bucket b --prefix key
lists versions and delete markers
findings.fix: State the idea first ('Enable versioning, then list versions and delete markers'). Then show the two commands, with a comment on each one.

findings.summary: The Block Public Access bullet packs four separate switches into one line, and the ARN failure bullet is cryptic.
findings.evidence: Four switches: block public ACLs, ignore public ACLs, block public policies, restrict public buckets; One ARN form only gives AccessDenied for the other
findings.fix: Show the four switches as a short 2-column list or table of switch and what it does. Reword the ARN bullet to 'Wrong ARN form → AccessDenied (bucket ARN for object actions, or bucket/* for bucket actions)'.

findings.summary: The 'Classes and Versioning' section mixes three topics (classes, versioning, lifecycle), and one bullet holds three ideas.
findings.evidence: 2. Classes and Versioning ... Versioning: suspend only, never removed ... Lifecycle: expire noncurrent, abort incomplete multipart; Flat keys; strong read-after-write; last writer wins
findings.fix: Split into separate sections for Classes, Versioning and Lifecycle. Put each of 'flat keys', 'strong read-after-write' and 'last writer wins' on its own line.

findings.summary: The handler code appears before its idea is stated; the one-line explanation of event and context comes after it.
findings.evidence: "def handler(event, context): ..." followed by "event = trigger JSON; context = request ID, time left, memory"
findings.fix: State "Handler takes event (trigger JSON) and context (request ID, time left, memory)" first, then show the code.

findings.summary: The section does not cover an outline point (missing "authenticate", "integration").
findings.evidence: Interview Point: HTTP API or REST API, and when? What shape must a proxy-integration response have? How does API Gateway authenticate callers before invoking Lambda?
findings.fix: Add the point with an explanation and an example.

findings.summary: The outline's Interview Point (SQS vs SNS vs EventBridge, why a visibility timeout under 6x risks duplicates, what a DLQ is for) is missing as a Q&A block, unlike pages 1-3 and 6.
findings.evidence: Page 4 ends with "Combine them / SNS fan-out into SQS queues: broadcast plus per-consumer buffering and retries." and has no "Interview Point" section
findings.fix: Add an Interview Point block with short answers: SQS decouples, SNS broadcasts, EventBridge routes by content; a short visibility timeout makes the message reappear while the first copy is still running, so a second copy runs; a DLQ catches poison messages after maxReceiveCount receives.

findings.summary: The EventBridge point is only named. Schema-based filtering is listed without saying what it does, and the page gives no example of routing by content.
findings.evidence: "Also cron/rate schedules, SaaS and AWS events, schema-based filtering"
findings.fix: Add one line or a small example: a rule pattern such as {"detail-type":["OrderPlaced"]} routes matching events to a target Lambda, and say what schema-based filtering adds.

findings.summary: One EventBridge bullet holds several unrelated ideas (schedules, event sources, filtering).
findings.evidence: "Also cron/rate schedules, SaaS and AWS events, schema-based filtering"
findings.fix: Split it into one-idea bullets: "Schedules: cron and rate", "Sources: SaaS and AWS events", "Schema-based filtering".

findings.summary: The section does not cover an outline point (missing "throughput", "workloads").
findings.evidence: Poor fit: long-running jobs over 15 minutes, steady high-throughput load (always-on containers or EC2 are cheaper), heavy low-latency needs, and large or GPU workloads
findings.fix: Add the point with an explanation and an example.

findings.summary: The outline's Interview Point (containers vs Lambda, stopping a recursive loop, why handlers must be idempotent) is not given as a Q&A block. The page only has a 'Remember' note on idempotency.
findings.evidence: Page 5 sections are "Poor Fit", "Common Mistakes" and "Remember / Idempotent"; there is no Interview Point
findings.fix: Add an Interview Point block: containers for jobs over 15 min, steady high load, low latency or GPU; stop a loop with reserved concurrency set to 0 or low, plus a billing alarm and separate buckets or prefixes; idempotent because retries and SQS deliver at least once.

findings.summary: The DB connection code is shown before the one-line idea that explains it, which only appears in the caption after the code.
findings.evidence: "conn = pymysql.connect(host=PROXY_HOST)" ... then "connect once per environment, outside the handler"
findings.fix: Put "Connect once per environment, outside the handler" as a bullet before the code block, and keep the code as the example.

findings.summary: The cheat sheet gives one API Gateway timeout of 29 s, but page 2 says HTTP API allows up to 30 s and REST API 29 s by default (raisable by quota).
findings.evidence: Page 6: "API Gateway timeout | 29 s" vs page 2: "REST API | 29 s default, raise by quota" and "HTTP API | 30 s max"
findings.fix: Split the cheat-sheet row into "REST API timeout | 29 s default" and "HTTP API timeout | 30 s max", matching page 2.

findings.summary: One bullet holds two ideas: replica promotion and replication lag.
findings.evidence: "Replica can be promoted to a standalone DB; lag is possible"
findings.fix: Split it into "Replica can be promoted to a standalone DB" and "Async replication means replica lag is possible".

findings.summary: The section does not cover an outline point (missing "configurable", "transaction").
findings.evidence: Automated backups: a daily snapshot plus transaction logs, on by default with 7 days of retention (configurable 1-35). Point-in-time restore works to any second within the window. Setting retention to 0 turns them off.
findings.fix: Add the point with an explanation and an example.

findings.summary: The mistake about disabling backups on a source with read replicas gives no reason, so a skimming learner cannot tell why it is a mistake.
findings.evidence: "Disabling backups on a source with read replicas"
findings.fix: Add the reason, for example "Retention 0 on a source breaks replication, since replicas need its backups/logs".

findings.summary: The Query code block comes before the one-line idea that explains it.
findings.evidence: "table.query(\n  KeyConditionExpression=Key('pk').eq('u1')\n  & Key('sk').begins_with('ORDER#'))" followed by "one partition, sort-key prefix"
findings.fix: Put "one partition, sort-key prefix" above the code block.

findings.summary: The cheat sheet and quiz say a Multi-AZ standby serves no reads, but page 1 says the Multi-AZ DB cluster standbys do serve reads, so the unqualified claim is inconsistent.
findings.evidence: Page 5: "Reads | None | Yes"; page 6: "No: the standby serves no reads; it only waits for failover." Page 1: "Multi-AZ DB cluster (two readable standbys) is the exception: standbys serve reads"
findings.fix: Qualify the claim as "Multi-AZ instance: standby serves no reads (DB cluster is the exception)" on pages 5 and 6, or name the Multi-AZ instance deployment explicitly in the tables.

overlaps: Intro 'What This Handbook Covers' chapters repeated in qr-ec2-vpc, qr-s3 and qr-rds-dynamodb
Cheat sheet closers in every chapter
Multi-AZ and availability zones appear in both qr-ec2-vpc and qr-rds-dynamodb
Bucket policies and IAM policy evaluation both cover resource-based policies
Least privilege and public-access security appear in qr-iam and qr-s3
